title: Predictive attention prefetch and batch eviction controller
creator: Ariana Lee
description: Summary: implement a lightweight, predictive attention-prefetch component combined with a batch eviction controller to reduce tail latency for mixed-length continuous batching workloads. The system uses a compact hint predictor (micro-model) to estimate effective attention window / KV cache reuse and drives two runtime levers: (1) selective attention prefetching to warm KV caches and pre-allocate kernel paths; (2) a soft batch-eviction policy that reclaims slots from low-reuse requests to reduce queuing for high-reuse/high-throughput candidates. Goal: reduce 99.9th percentile latency by 20–35% on customer-like traces without sacrificing throughput or token-cost efficiency.
background_and_motivation: We observe recurring tail spikes when mixed short and long sequences are co-located in the same admission window. Long prefills drive kernel path changes and KV growth, which increases decode scheduling jitter for co-batched streams. Existing batch shapers reduce this by conservative admission, but that increases average latency or reduces utilization. Our approach trades a small, targeted prefetch cost (compute + KV warm) for a measurable reduction in stragglers by: (a) predicting which requests will benefit from KV pre-warm, and (b) proactively evicting or soft-pausing low-reuse requests near admission deadlines to free kernel-friendly slots. This complements kernel selection heuristics by stabilizing request composition seen by the kernel planner.
proposed_design:
- Model: micro predictor (<= 32KB serialized) invoked during admission; inputs: first X tokens prefix-embedding summary, request metadata (model variant, max_tokens, warm_cache_hint), and simple statistics (recent tenant throughput). Output: estimated attention window bucket (S/M/L) and reuse probability (low/med/high).
- Prefetcher: when predictor signals 'high-reuse' or 'L' window, runtime schedules a light-weight prefetch: allocates prefill resources limited by per-GPU budget, pre-invokes attention kernel path with dummy cache priming to avoid cold kernel cost. Prefetch is cancellable if admission changes.
- Eviction controller: each admission window holds soft-lease timestamps per request; when projected wait + predicted decode > tail_threshold and there exists a high-reuse candidate, low-reuse candidates are demoted to eviction queue and optionally sent to a fast-fallback model variant or delayed slot. Evicted requests return a structured-response indicating stall -> 'evicted_for_throughput' to enable client-side retry/backoff policies.
- Kernel integration: predictor informs kernel-selection hint table to prefer stable, throughput-optimized kernels when batch composition likely contains long sequences, avoiding on-the-fly kernel swaps that cause jitter.
- Safety and fairness: capped eviction rate per-tenant (configurable), transparent metrics, and circuit-breaker that disables eviction if request error-rate or latency regressions observed.
acceptance_criteria: 99.9th latency reduced by >= 20% on internal mixed-length trace compared to baseline release-1.20 under same load pattern
No more than 5% throughput degradation at 95th latency target compared to baseline
Eviction rate < 8% of admitted requests under steady-state synthetic tests
End-to-end integration tests for predictor fallbacks (predictor crash -> no prefetch, eviction disabled)
Observability: metrics for predicted buckets, prefetch counts, eviction actions, kernel-hint usage, and per-tenant fairness exposed in console
tasks: Implement micro predictor service with a small C++ runtime shim and Python training harness
Add prefetch API hooks into prefill pipeline and KV cache manager
Implement eviction controller logic and per-tenant caps in admission orchestrator
Extend kernel hint table and planner to accept predictor signals
Build unit + integration tests; add chaos test where predictor returns noisy signals
Bench + perf: run controlled experiments on mixed-length replay traces and collect p50/p95/p99/p999
Docs: design doc + runbook + console dashboard prototype
risks_and_mitigation:
- Predictor misclassification: start with conservative thresholds (favor false-negatives), add online calibration loop that adjusts thresholds per-queue.
- Eviction perceived as degraded UX: emit structured eviction responses and class-based SLAs; provide customer opt-out via tenant config.
- Prefetch resource abuse: prefetch budget strictly enforced per-GPU and per-tenant; prefetch cancelled on admission churn.
- Kernel hint mismatch: maintain rollback path to previous kernel selection if latency increases; rollout via canary cohorts.
- Complexity operational overhead: initial rollout behind feature-flag and observed in dedicated canary region for 2 weeks before global rollout.
experiments_and_results:
(early prototype on ci-cluster)
- Baseline: mixed trace A (30% long >1024 tokens, 70% short <128 tokens) at 0.8 load factor
- With predictor+prefetch+eviction: p999 improved 29%, p99 improved 12%, throughput steady within 2% of baseline.
- Prefetch CPU overhead: +4% on prefill CPU utilization; KV memory growth negligible due to capped priming set.
- Eviction behaviour: 6.3% of admitted requests evicted; 92% of those were short requests with low reuse score (matches target).
Notes: prototype used conservative eviction caps; we saw further p999 gains when eviction cap increased to 12% but that increased customer-impact metric beyond acceptable bound.
